artboards.title: Proposed — checking one bill, one supplier searched
Proposed — sound, empty, never started, and failed to read
Proposed — one bill, and paying it, on the phone

annotations.text:
WHAT I TOOK FROM YOUR ANSWERS

You asked for all four jobs at once — find and print one bill, check a bill is right, pay from here, and read what the shop has been spending. That is a lot for one screen, so it is layered rather than crammed: a strip that answers the spending question in four figures, a band that answers the checking question and nothing else, and one list whose rows open into the bill itself.

1. THE UNIT HERE IS ONE BILL. Creditors' unit is one supplier. That division is stated on the screen, in the rail, because the two screens have overlapped in the owner's head since Creditors shipped. A payment recorded on either shows on both, and who to pay first is decided in exactly one place.

2. CHECKING IS THE POINT, so it is a panel with a header like every other region — not a red slab. Four faults, each named, each with the money at stake and ONE act. And it says so when everything is sound (page 2), because a band that only appears when something is wrong leaves you unable to tell "nothing wrong" from "not looked at".

3. THE TWO KINDS ARE SPLIT — bought for an order, bought for the shelf — as a segment, so the column that meant two different things per row is gone.

4. THE ROW OPENS INTO THE BILL. Today the only way to read what is on a bill is to press Print and open a print dialog. That is the single worst thing about this screen. Now the row opens in place onto the lines, each priced against what the same goods last cost you from that same supplier.

5. THE ACCENT APPEARS ONCE — the one act inside the one open row.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Creditors, Chase debts, Follow-ups and Consignment. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. YOU CANNOT READ A BILL WITHOUT PRINTING IT. Both the doc-number link and the printer button call printPurchaseInvoicesA5(). On the screen whose whole subject is supplier bills, the contents of a bill are not on screen at all. Everything else here is a symptom of that.

2. TWELVE COLUMNS THAT DO NOT FIT. At 1440px the last three — Payment status, Paid / collected, and the four buttons on every row — are off the right edge, reachable only by scrolling the table sideways. The row's own actions are the part you cannot see.

3. ONE COLUMN, TWO MEANINGS. "Paid / collected" shows how much of the CLIENT'S order has been collected on an order-linked bill, and how much has been PAID to the supplier on a restock. The code's own comment admits three of four rows read "0% paid, which is not collection". A blue bar appears on a screen whose palette has no blue.

4. A NEGATIVE BALANCE PRESENTED AS "SETTLED". PINV‑0231 shows Balance due UGX ‑180,000 with a green Settled chip. The shop paid 180,000 more than it was billed and the screen calls that finished.

5. THE DUPLICATE WARNING IS A RED SLAB with three paragraphs of prose, permanently at the top, and it is the only check the screen makes. Its button voids without ever showing you the two bills side by side.

6. NOTHING IS CHECKED ABOUT THE MONEY. Nothing looks at whether a price is above what you have ever paid that supplier, whether a bill has a delivery behind it, or whether more has left the drawer than was asked. Every figure needed for all three is already on file.

7. NO POSITION AT ALL. No strip, no totals except a footer row you reach by scrolling. The screen cannot answer "what has this shop been spending, and with whom".

8. A 190-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH IN THE PAGE HEAD, unmeasured, open above the work — and it describes how bills are GENERATED, which is the one thing the owner never has to do.

9. CONTROLS THAT DO NOT LOOK LIKE CONTROLS. Floating labels over a select, a bare checkbox nudged with padding-bottom:9px, and a "Bulk operation" dropdown on its own row above a Print list button on the other side.

10. FOUR ICON BUTTONS PER ROW, unlabelled, one of which — the ✕ — does not void on a delivery bill but takes the goods back off the shelf and reopens the order. Only a title attribute says so.

11. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES: 13.5 / 12.5 / 11.5 / 10.5 type, radius 10, a drop shadow where depth in this app is hairlines, and #3B6FB6 — a blue that is not in the 23.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

THE STRIP ANSWERS THE SPENDING QUESTION IN FOUR FIGURES. Billed to you; paid out against them; still owed — which names Creditors rather than pretending to rank anything; and needs your eye, in bills rather than shillings, because four bills is the thing you act on and 3,822,400 is not one sum you can do anything with. It is the only crimson on the screen.

WHAT NEEDS YOUR EYE. Four checks, all derivable from what is already on file, all run every time the screen draws:
· the same delivery billed twice — already implemented, now with one act, "Compare the two", because voiding a bill you have not looked at is exactly the mistake;
· a line priced above anything you have ever paid THAT supplier for THAT line;
· a bill with no delivery behind it on the stock record;
· money paid out beyond what was billed — the negative balance the current screen calls "settled".
Each is one line, one sentence of evidence, the money, and one act. Amber where a person must look; crimson only where the shop is out of pocket.

AND IT SAYS WHAT IT DOES NOT CHECK. Age is not checked here — the note at the foot of the band sends that to Creditors by name. Nor is whether the goods that came were the ones ordered, nor whether a price you have never paid before is fair; the rail says so and sends the second to Compare prices. A checking screen that does not state its own boundary is a screen you cannot trust the silence of.

THE SPLIT IS A SEGMENT: All · For an order · For the shelf. The column that meant two things per row is gone; every row instead says plainly which kind it is, and an order-linked row names the order it was raised from.

THE ROW OPENS ONTO THE BILL. Line, qty, unit price, WHAT YOU LAST PAID with the day, the difference, line total. That column is the whole check, and it is the reason a bill can now be argued before it is paid rather than after. A dearer line is banded crimson; a cheaper one is verdigris and is worth seeing too. The footer carries billed / paid / still owed and the acts, with the accent on the one that matters for that bill.

EVERY ACT SAYS WHAT IT WILL DO. "Void" on a delivery bill becomes "Undo the delivery", and the rail carries the consequence in full — the goods come back off the shelf and the order goes back to waiting — rather than hiding it in a title attribute.

THE RAIL CARRIES THE READING. What this screen is and what Creditors is; what is checked and what is not; what the shop bought in the range, split by kind; and where the money went, by supplier. That last panel is the "what have I been spending" answer, and it is four lines rather than a report.

HEIGHT: everything above the list went from a 190-character paragraph plus a red slab to a strip and a band, and the first four bills are on the first screen.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. "YOU LAST PAID" IS THE HIGHEST YOU HAVE PAID that supplier for that line, not the most recent. Highest catches a creep that "most recent" would let through one step at a time; most recent is the fairer comparison in a rising market. Say the word and it is one comparator.

2. THE FOURTH CHECK — "a bill with nothing received against it" — is the least certain of the four. It is sound on a bill raised from your own purchase order. On one entered by hand it may simply mean the stock was counted in separately, in which case it will cry wolf. It may want a "this is fine" dismissal that sticks.

3. I HAVE NOT PUT AGE OR BROKEN PROMISES HERE, deliberately, and said so on screen. If you would rather this screen also showed which bills are past a day you named, it is one more column — but then two screens rank the same money and they will drift.

4. BULK OPERATIONS ARE GONE from the toolbar. Print selected / void selected / unvoid selected were three items behind a dropdown above a checkbox column, and voiding in bulk on this screen can take goods off the shelf in bulk. Print survives as "Print these N", which follows the filter. If you genuinely bulk-void, say so and it comes back — with the delivery consequence spelled out per row.

5. SEVEN OTHER SUPPLIERS ARE SUMMED IN ONE LINE in the rail rather than listed. If the spending read matters more than I have assumed, that panel wants to be a screen of its own rather than four rows.

6. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the payment modal, the bill-correction modal, the A5 printed sheet, and the CSV — beyond the printed sheet needing to say which filter it was printed under.

CHECKING ONE BILL, WITH A SUPPLIER SEARCHED →

THE BAND FOLDS TO THE ONE YOU ARE WORKING and says the other three are folded, with the way back. It does not vanish, and it does not stay at full height arguing with the bill underneath it.

THE FILTER IS VISIBLE IN THREE PLACES — the segment, an amber chip with its own ✕, and the note under the list which says how many are hidden and what they came to. Print says "Print these 3".

THE FIGURES ABOVE THE LIST DO NOT MOVE for a search or a segment, and the note says so in those words. The existing code's comment on the Creditors screen gives the reason: a position that shrinks because somebody left a filter on is a position nobody can trust.

THE COMPARISON IS THE POINT OF THE OPEN ROW. Two lines banded crimson, one unchanged, one cheaper. Under the table, one amber note that refuses to give a verdict: iron sheets have moved with the market twice this year and the registry has not been refreshed since 12 July, so this may simply be the going rate. "You have not paid this much before" is a fact; "you are being overcharged" would be an invention, and the app's own law is derived, never invented.

THE ACT IS SCOPED AND SAID. Correcting a price changes what is owed and what the goods cost you. It moves nothing on or off the shelf — that is Undo the delivery, a different act — and it does not touch the price registry, so if this IS the new going rate the note sends you to Compare prices to record it.

A VOIDED ROW IS NAMED, NOT HIDDEN. Struck through, its money struck through, and the reason on the row: "Delivery undone — the goods came back off the shelf."

THE RAIL BECOMES THE SUPPLIER while one is searched: what you have bought from them, what is open, when you last paid them, and the two doors to their card and their prices.

THE FOUR STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN →

1. NOTHING TO LOOK AT is the state that does not exist today, and it is the most important one on this screen. If the check band only ever appears when something is wrong, its absence is ambiguous: you cannot tell "nothing wrong" from "not run". So a clean check says so, in one sentence, with the two figures that make an empty finding meaningful.

2. NOTHING IN THIS RANGE names the nearest bill outside it and offers both doors. Today this says "No purchase invoices in this range." and stops — leaving you to guess whether the range is wrong or the book is empty.

3. NEVER HAD ONE is worded differently, because a shop that has never been billed has not "found nothing"; it has not begun. And it names BOTH ways a bill comes into being — an order marked invoiced, or a delivery received against your own purchase order. The current copy names only the first, which is why a restock bill appearing out of nowhere is confusing.

4. THE BILLS WOULD NOT LOAD does not exist at all today: a failed read and an empty book both render "No purchase invoices yet." The app's own law says a failure must name itself. So it says what failed, when the last good read was and what it held, that these are not today's figures — and it turns Record payment OFF, because money must never be posted against a bill nobody can see.

In the app only one of the four is ever on screen. They are stacked here to compare the wording.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 14–16px row padding, 44px hit targets, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS NOT THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are working down the range deciding what is sound. On a phone, a supplier's man is standing in front of you with a delivery note. So: the 2×2 strip, then the check band as ONE tappable line rather than four — you are not auditing in a yard, you are being told there are four to come back to — then search, then the split, then cards.

THE CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON. The card is the tap target; the accent lives once, in the docked navy bar in the thumb zone, the pattern Creditors and Follow-ups already ship. It names who is standing in front of you so the default is right without reading the list.

YOU SAID PAYMENT SHOULD BE POSSIBLE HERE, so the second screen is the bill itself: the lines with the price comparison carried over — banded, not tabulated, because five columns do not survive 390px — the three figures, and Pay this bill docked. The dock says what is still owed beside the button, so the figure and the act are read together.

MONEY NEVER TRUNCATES. Line names give way with an ellipsis; not one figure does.
